slides.text:
Go programs share a record by pointing at it instead of copying it. A function, a list or a tree node can all reach the same struct.

You will create a pointer to a struct, reach its fields, share it, copy it, pass it to functions and compare it.
The examples use small structs: a group of named fields, declared with `type` and `struct`. Structs get their own course later, so here you only need their shape.

A literal builds a struct. A **keyed** literal names each field, a **positional** one lists the values in field order. A dot reaches a field.

The next modules use all three.

With a pointer to a struct, a dot reaches a field directly. Go follows the pointer for you.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
p = address of a Player
p.score = 5
(*p).score = 5   same thing
*p = the whole Player

slides.text:
Copying a pointer copies only the address, so both reach one struct. Following the pointer in an assignment copies the whole struct.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
b = a        one struct, two names
c = copy of *a   two structs

exercises.title: Two names, one struct
exercises.guide: Copy a pointer and see both names reach the same struct.

chunks.guide: Make a pointer, then a second one from it.

notes.text: Copies the address only: no new struct exists

chunks.guide: Change a field through the second pointer and read it through the first.

exercises.title: Copy the struct
exercises.guide: Follow the pointer to get an independent copy.

chunks.guide: Dereferencing a pointer in an assignment copies the struct.

notes.text: c is a plain Player, separate from the original

chunks.guide: Change the copy: the original stays as it was.

exercises.title: Alias and clone
exercises.guide: Make alias share the player and clone be a separate copy, so the final score is 50.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `b` points at the same struct as `a`, so the 7 shows in both. `c` is a copy, so the 9 stays in `c`.

slides.text:
A struct pointer can be a parameter, so the function changes the caller's struct, and a function can return a pointer to a new struct. Comparing pointers compares addresses, comparing the structs behind them compares fields.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
takes a pointer -> changes the caller's
returns a pointer -> a new struct
a == b      same address?
*a == *b    same fields?

exercises.title: Change it in a function
exercises.guide: A function that takes a pointer to a struct changes the caller's struct.

chunks.guide: The parameter is a pointer, so the change reaches the caller.

notes.text: Receives the address of a player, not a copy

chunks.guide: Pass the pointer in and read the score afterwards.

exercises.title: Return a pointer
exercises.guide: A function can build a struct and hand back its address.

chunks.guide: Build the player inside and return a pointer to it.

notes.text: Safe: Go keeps the struct alive after the function ends

chunks.guide: Use the pointer you got back.

exercises.title: Fix the return type
exercises.guide: Make newPlayer give back a pointer to a new player.

exercises.title: Compare pointers
exercises.guide: Two pointers are equal only when they aim at the same struct.

chunks.guide: Two separate players with the same contents.
Compare the pointers, then the structs they point at.

notes.text: Compares every field of both structs

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `a` and `b` are different structs, so their addresses differ. `c` is the same address as `a`. The structs `*a` and `*b` hold equal fields.
